stem: A company runs virtual machines on a public cloud provider's IaaS platform. Who is responsible for applying operating system security patches to those VMs?

options.text: The customer
options.why: Under IaaS the provider supplies compute, storage and network. Everything from the guest operating system upward belongs to the customer.

options.text: The cloud provider
options.why: The provider patches the hypervisor and the physical infrastructure. The guest OS inside your VM is yours.

options.text: Shared equally between both parties
options.why: The matrix assigns each layer to one party. It does not split a single layer.

options.text: Whichever party the contract names, with no default
options.why: The service model sets the default division, which is precisely what the responsibility matrix documents.

stem: Customer records stored in a SaaS CRM were exposed because a sharing permission was set to 'anyone with the link'. Who is responsible?

options.text: The customer, because configuration and access are never transferred to the provider
options.why: Data, identity and configuration remain the customer's responsibility in every service model, SaaS included.

options.text: The provider, because in SaaS they manage the entire stack
options.why: They manage the application, the runtime and the infrastructure. They do not choose your sharing settings.

options.text: The provider, because the exposure was through their application's feature
options.why: The feature worked as designed. The customer configured it to share publicly.

options.text: Neither, since no system was breached
options.why: A data exposure is a security incident whether or not anything was technically compromised.

stem: A trading platform has an RTO of 30 minutes. Which recovery site is appropriate?

options.text: A hot site
options.why: Only a hot site, with hardware, software and current data already running, can restore service inside 30 minutes.

options.text: A warm site
options.why: A warm site has the equipment but not current data. Restoring and validating it takes hours at best.

options.text: A cold site
options.why: A cold site is space, power and connectivity. Standing it up takes days or weeks.

options.text: An offsite backup vault
options.why: Storing media offsite protects the data. It provides nowhere to run the platform.

stem: A charity can tolerate several days of downtime and has a very limited budget. Which recovery option fits?

options.text: A cold site
options.why: With a tolerant RTO and a tight budget, paying only for space, power and connectivity is the appropriate trade.

options.text: A hot site
options.why: A hot site is the most expensive option by a wide margin, and the RTO does not require it.

options.text: A warm site
options.why: Reasonable in the middle of the range, and it still means paying to keep hardware and software standing by.

options.text: Clustering across two data centres
options.why: That is a high availability design, the most expensive approach of all, for an organisation that can accept days of downtime.

stem: A database must continue serving requests with its session state intact if one node fails. Which design meets this?

options.text: Clustering, so the nodes act as one logical system sharing state
options.why: Clustering is defined by shared state and workload takeover, which is what preserving sessions across a node failure requires.

options.text: A load balancer distributing connections across independent nodes
options.why: Load balancing spreads requests and the nodes do not share state, so the sessions on the failed node are lost.

options.text: Replication to a standby copy
options.why: Replication keeps a second copy current. On its own it does not provide automatic takeover with live session state.

options.text: Nightly backups to a second data centre
options.why: Backups restore data eventually. They provide no continuity at all.

stem: A web farm is struggling under traffic growth. Requests must be spread across all available servers. Which device is required?

options.text: A load balancer
options.why: Distributing incoming requests across a pool of servers for capacity is exactly what a load balancer does.

options.text: A cluster manager
options.why: Clustering makes servers act as one logical system with shared state, which is not what spreading stateless web requests needs.

options.text: A jump server
options.why: A jump server is a controlled entry point for administrators, not a traffic distributor.

options.text: A forward proxy
options.why: A forward proxy handles internal users going out to the internet, the opposite direction.

stem: A company replicates its file server continuously to a second data centre. Ransomware encrypts the primary. What happens?

options.text: The encrypted files replicate to the secondary, so both copies are unusable
options.why: Replication faithfully copies every change, including malicious ones. It protects against hardware and site failure, not against corruption.

options.text: The secondary is unaffected because replication is one way
options.why: One way is the direction of the copy, which is exactly why the encryption travels from primary to secondary.

options.text: The secondary retains previous versions and can be rolled back
options.why: That is versioned backup or snapshot behaviour. Plain replication keeps only the current state.

options.text: Replication halts automatically when corruption is detected
options.why: Replication does not evaluate whether changes are legitimate. It has no idea the file was encrypted rather than edited.

stem: A transaction system must be recoverable to any moment, not just to the last backup. Which method supports this?

options.text: Journaling every change so the log can be replayed to a chosen point
options.why: A change journal allows point in time recovery at very fine granularity, which is how a near zero RPO is achieved.

options.text: Hourly snapshots
options.why: Snapshots give you the hourly points, and nothing between them.

options.text: Nightly full backups
options.why: That gives you one recovery point per day, which is an RPO of up to 24 hours.

options.text: Continuous replication to a standby
options.why: Replication gives you the current state at the standby. It does not let you choose an earlier moment.

stem: A bank must process sensitive records on a cloud host such that even a privileged administrator of that host cannot read them during processing. Which protection is required?

options.text: A secure enclave or confidential computing environment
options.why: Data in use must be decrypted to be processed. A hardware enclave keeps it protected from the host OS and its administrators even then.

options.text: Full disk encryption on the host
options.why: That protects data at rest on a powered off disk. Once the system is running and the volume is mounted, an administrator reads it freely.

options.text: TLS 1.3 for all connections to the host
options.why: TLS protects data in transit. It ends at the host, where the data is decrypted.

options.text: Tokenising the records before storage
options.why: Useful, and the application still has to detokenise to process the real values, which returns you to the data in use problem.

stem: A laptop is stolen from a car while powered off. Which control protected the data on it?

options.text: Full disk encryption, which protects data at rest
options.why: A powered off encrypted disk is unreadable without the key, which is exactly the data at rest scenario.

options.text: TLS on all the laptop's connections
options.why: TLS protects data in transit across a network. It is irrelevant to a disk in a thief's hands.

options.text: A secure enclave protecting data in use
options.why: Data in use means data loaded in memory during processing. The machine is off.

options.text: A host based firewall
options.why: A firewall filters network traffic. It does nothing for physical possession of the disk.

stem: A company holds payment card numbers. Asked to state the DATA TYPE, which answer is correct?

options.text: Regulated data
options.why: Card data is governed by external requirements, which makes its type regulated. Its classification would be a separate label such as restricted.

options.text: Restricted
options.why: Restricted is a classification level, describing handling sensitivity. The question asked for the type.

options.text: Confidential
options.why: Also a classification level, on the wrong axis for this question.

options.text: Critical
options.why: Another classification level. All three of these distractors are on the classification axis.

stem: A beverage company's unpublished formula, protected by secrecy rather than by registration, is best described as which data type?

options.text: A trade secret
options.why: Its value depends on it remaining unknown, and it is protected by keeping it secret rather than by a registered right.

options.text: Intellectual property protected by patent
options.why: A patent requires publication in exchange for a time limited monopoly, which is the opposite approach to a trade secret.

options.text: Regulated data
options.why: No external regulator governs a recipe. Regulated data means data whose handling is prescribed by law or standard.

options.text: Confidential
options.why: That is the classification you would assign it, not the type of data it is.

stem: A distributed workforce must receive identical web filtering, CASB and zero trust access policy wherever they connect, without routing traffic back to headquarters. Which architecture fits?

options.text: SASE
options.why: SASE delivers network and security services together from the cloud edge, so policy follows the user rather than the office.

options.text: SD-WAN
options.why: SD-WAN intelligently routes traffic between sites. It is connectivity, and it does not inherently carry the security stack.

options.text: A site to site IPSec VPN mesh
options.why: That provides encrypted connectivity between fixed sites and no policy enforcement for roaming users.

options.text: A reverse proxy at headquarters
options.why: A reverse proxy fronts inbound traffic to your servers. It does not govern users' outbound access from anywhere.

stem: Which statement correctly compares containers with virtual machines?

options.text: Containers share the host kernel, which makes them lighter and their isolation weaker
options.why: The shared kernel explains both the millisecond startup and the fact that a kernel flaw affects every container on the host.

options.text: Containers each run a full guest operating system, like a lightweight VM
options.why: That is what a virtual machine does. A container packages only the application and its dependencies.

options.text: Containers provide stronger isolation than virtual machines because of their smaller attack surface
options.why: The image is smaller and the isolation boundary is weaker, because the kernel is shared rather than virtualised.

options.text: Containers require a hypervisor, virtual machines do not
options.why: Reversed. Virtual machines run on a hypervisor; containers run on a container runtime over the shared kernel.

stem: An attacker breaks out of a guest virtual machine and executes code on the hypervisor. What is this called, and why does it matter so much?

options.text: VM escape, because it exposes every other guest on that host
options.why: The hypervisor is the isolation boundary for all guests. Compromising it collapses the separation between every tenant on the machine.

options.text: Resource reuse, because memory is shared between guests
options.why: Resource reuse is when data lingers in memory or storage reallocated to another tenant. That is a leak, not a breakout.

options.text: Container escape, because the kernel is shared
options.why: Container escape breaks out to a shared host kernel. Virtual machines do not share a kernel.

options.text: Privilege escalation, confined to the affected guest
options.why: The defining feature is that it is not confined to the guest. It reaches the host.

stem: A data centre must experience no interruption at all during a mains failure and must stay running for at least 48 hours. What is required?

options.text: A UPS and a generator together
options.why: The UPS carries the load instantly through the seconds the generator needs to start, and the generator sustains the site for as long as there is fuel.

options.text: A generator alone
options.why: A generator has a start delay. Without a UPS, everything drops for those seconds, which violates 'no interruption at all'.

options.text: A UPS alone, sized for 48 hours
options.why: Battery capacity at data centre load is measured in minutes. Sizing one for 48 hours is not practical.

options.text: Dual mains feeds from the same substation
options.why: Two feeds from one substation share its failure. It is not a substitute for local generation.

stem: All administrative access to the production segment must pass through one hardened, heavily monitored host. What is this called?

options.text: A jump server
options.why: A jump server, or bastion host, is the single controlled and audited entry point administrators use to reach a protected zone.

options.text: A reverse proxy
options.why: A reverse proxy fronts servers for external users arriving at published services, not administrators entering a zone.

options.text: A forward proxy
options.why: A forward proxy handles internal users going outbound to the internet.

options.text: A screened subnet
options.why: A screened subnet is a network zone for publicly reachable services, not a single administrative entry host.

stem: An electronically controlled door secures a server room. Fire regulations require occupants to be able to leave during a power failure. How should the door fail?

options.text: Fail-open, so occupants can evacuate
options.why: Life safety overrides security. A door that traps people during a fire is not an acceptable control at any sensitivity level.

options.text: Fail-closed, because the server room is highly sensitive
options.why: The reflexive security answer, and here it is dangerous and prohibited by fire regulations.

options.text: Fail-closed, with a manual override key held by security
options.why: Depending on someone locating a key during a fire is not an evacuation route.

options.text: It should remain in whatever state it was in
options.why: Undefined behaviour is not a failure mode. The design must choose one deliberately.

stem: A firewall protecting a cardholder data environment loses power. Which failure mode is appropriate?

options.text: Fail-closed, denying traffic until the device is restored
options.why: For a regulated, highly sensitive segment, an outage is preferable to passing uninspected and unfiltered traffic.

options.text: Fail-open, to preserve availability of the payment service
options.why: That leaves the cardholder environment exposed with no filtering, which is the outcome the control exists to prevent.

options.text: Fail-open, since a firewall outage is a safety issue
options.why: Life safety considerations apply to physical egress, not to network filtering.

options.text: Either is acceptable provided it is documented
options.why: Documentation does not make an inappropriate failure mode appropriate for a regulated segment.

stem: An engineering team states that their SCADA network is air gapped. An audit finds a single firewalled link to the corporate network used for historian data. How should this be assessed?

options.text: It is not air gapped; it is logically segmented and should be described and defended as such
options.why: An air gap means no connection exists. One firewalled link is a controlled path, and treating it as an air gap leads to weaker controls than a connected network requires.

options.text: It remains air gapped, because the link is firewalled
options.why: A firewall filters a connection. It does not remove one.

options.text: It is physically isolated, since the SCADA hardware is separate
options.why: Separate hardware with a network link between them is not isolation.

options.text: It is microsegmented
options.why: Microsegmentation applies policy per workload. One perimeter link between two networks is not that.

stem: A genuinely air gapped system was infected with malware. What is the most likely vector?

options.text: Removable media carried across the gap
options.why: With no network path, data still has to move somehow, and USB media is the classic route into an air gapped environment.

options.text: A phishing email opened by an operator
options.why: An air gapped system has no mail connectivity, which is what the gap means.

options.text: Exploitation of an internet facing service
options.why: There is no internet facing service. If there were, it would not be air gapped.

options.text: A compromised VPN credential
options.why: A VPN is a network path, which an air gapped system by definition does not have.

stem: An organisation defines its entire cloud environment in version controlled templates that are applied automatically. What is the main security benefit?

options.text: Configuration is consistent, reviewable and reproducible, so drift and one-off mistakes are prevented
options.why: Infrastructure as code makes the environment auditable and repeatable, and changes go through review like any other code.

options.text: The cloud provider becomes responsible for the resulting configuration
options.why: Configuration is the customer's responsibility in every service model. Automating it does not transfer it.

options.text: It removes the need to patch the resulting systems
options.why: It makes rebuilding patched systems easier. It does not remove the requirement.

options.text: It provides isolation equivalent to an air gap
options.why: IaC describes how infrastructure is defined. It says nothing about network separation.
